## ppwr-evidence

Stores the files suppliers upload, and hands them back by address.

`ppwr-store` keeps the rows. This keeps the bytes those rows point at. A document row whose file vanished when the execution ended is not much of an audit trail.

**Contract**

In: `{ op, uri, filename, mime_type, content_b64, request_id }`

Out: `{ ok, uri, sha256, byte_size, mime_type, filename, content_b64, backend, request_id }`

An address is the content hash, `evidence://<sha256>`, never a path. Paths move. If a row pointed at `/home/node/.n8n/evidence/ab12...` and somebody reorganised the volume, every verdict already reached would lose its evidence.

The hash is computed here from the bytes, not taken from the caller. On the way back out the file is hashed again and checked against the address it was fetched by. If those disagree the execution fails.

Uploading the same file twice costs one write. Same bytes, same address, second write skipped.

**Setup**

Evidence lives under `~/.n8n-files`. n8n 2.x blocks its own `.n8n` folder and confines nodes to that directory unless you set `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO`. Give it a volume so it survives the container:

`- n8n-evidence:/home/node/.n8n-files`

Then once: `docker exec -u node n8n mkdir -p /home/node/.n8n-files/ppwr-evidence`

Code nodes are built from `src/evidence/` by `npm run bundle` and swapped in at deploy. Editing them on the canvas will not survive.

### Put

Bytes in, address out. The same document uploaded twice resolves to the same file and the second write costs nothing.

### Get

Address in, bytes out, hashed on the way past. A mismatch fails the execution.

nodes.name: Configuration
nodes.notes:
Under ~/.n8n-files, deliberately. Verified against a live instance: n8n 2.x restricts node file access to that directory by default, and blocks its own .n8n folder outright, so any other path fails with "Access to the file is not allowed" until an operator sets N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO. This default works on an untouched instance.

It still has to be a volume, or the evidence behind every verdict dies with the container.

nodes.name: Evidence to binary for write
nodes.notes: Converted a second time. Verified against a live instance: the Crypto node returns an item with no binary, so the bytes it just hashed cannot be written by anything downstream of it. Binary survives exactly one hop.

nodes.name: Base64 to binary for hashing
nodes.notes: One read from disk, then a round trip through base64 so the digest still covers the bytes that came off the disk. extractFromFile returns an item with no binary, so the hash needs its own copy.
